summary: Help 5–7 year olds appreciate that a volcanic eruption is a powerful, dramatic event that reshapes the land around a volcano, and that over time life returns, helped by volcanic ash that slowly breaks down into fertile soil. The core evidence is comparing the landscape before and after an eruption using pictures. Aim for awe, not fear: an eruption changes the land, it does not ruin it forever. Keep named case studies (e.g. Pompeii) and eruption types for older topics. Assume children can already name a volcano and lava.
misconceptions: 'An eruption destroys everything forever and nothing grows back' — land recovers; weathered ash makes very fertile soil
'Eruptions only destroy' — they also BUILD land, new rock, taller mountains and even new islands
'Lava is the only thing an eruption does' — ash, new landforms and changed terrain are also part of the power (kept simple here)
'Every eruption is a giant explosion' — eruptions vary in power (types come later); here just appreciate they can be dramatic
'The changed land stays lifeless' — plants and animals return over time

activities.title: Press to erupt, then compare before and after
steps: Look at a calm scene: a green valley with a quiet mountain. Say what you see.
Press an 'erupt' trigger and watch what happens: lava pours out and cools into new black rock, ash drifts down and blankets the fields, and the cone grows taller.
Flip a before/after toggle (or drag a reveal across the scene) to switch between the original land and the changed land.
Tap 'what changed?' hotspots and name each difference out loud: new black rock, ash cover, and a taller cone.
Advance a gentle time slider labelled 'and later…' and watch green shoots push up through the ash.
Answer aloud: 'Did the land grow back? Why do plants grow well here now?'
activities.insight: An eruption is powerful and can completely change the landscape; the land is reshaped and covered, but over time plants return and the volcanic soil is very fertile — so an eruption both reshapes and renews the land.

activities.title: Before / after / later picture pairs with tap-to-reveal
steps: Study a paired illustration or real photographs: a green valley, then the same place as an ash-covered plain with new lava rock.
Tap points on the 'after' picture and name each change (ash cover, black lava rock, changed hill shape).
Lift an 'and later…' flap (or tap a third 'years later' picture) to see plants returning on the fertile ash.
Say in your own words how the land is different and what came back.
activities.insight: Comparing before and after pictures shows that an eruption changes the shape and surface of the land, and a later picture shows that life returns over time.

activities.title: Eyewitness account: the valley before and the morning after
steps: Listen to a friendly character describe what the valley looked like before the eruption, and what it looked like the morning after.
Ask the character your own question, for example 'Did it grow back?'
Listen to the reassuring, true answer that plants return over time on the rich ash soil, and retell one thing that changed and one thing that came back.
activities.insight: An eruption is a dramatic event that changed the place the character describes, and the land recovers over time — so the feeling is awe, not terror.

activities.title: Check: match before to after and spot what changed
steps: Match each 'before' landscape to its correct 'after' landscape.
Answer: 'How did the eruption change the land?' and reject a 'nothing changed' option by explaining what actually changed.
Answer: 'What happens to the land years later?' choosing the option where plants return.
activities.insight: I can identify that an eruption changes the land and that life returns later, distinguishing real change from 'nothing happened'.

checkQuestion: After a volcano erupts and covers the land in ash and lava, everything nearby is buried and black. A friend says, 'That land is ruined forever — nothing will ever grow there again.' Do you agree? What happens to the land around a volcano after an eruption?
checkAnswer: The friend is wrong. An eruption is powerful and dramatically changes the land — burying and reshaping the area — but over time plants grow back, often very well, because volcanic ash makes the soil rich. The land is changed, not ruined forever.
